result:
The hour before dawn belongs to no one. Streetlights still burn, but their glow has grown pale, embarrassed by the faint blue seeping through the edges of the sky. In this liminal space, the world seems to hold its breath. Birds have not yet begun their morning arguments. The air carries the cool, mineral smell of night reluctantly giving way to morning.

I have always found this hour more honest than midnight. Midnight is dramatic — it performs darkness, invites insomnia and grand thoughts that evaporate by morning. But the pre-dawn hour makes no promises. It simply exists, transitional and utterly unbothered, a hinge between what was and what will be.

Perhaps that is why writers and insomniacs and early risers share a quiet, secret kinship. We have all witnessed this unguarded moment, when the world forgets to be observed. A cat crossing an empty street pauses mid-step, entirely unafraid. A bakery's lights flicker on, the first act of a day that no one has scripted yet.

There is a lesson buried here, I think: that transitions deserve more attention than destinations. We celebrate arrivals and mourn departures, but the space between — the slow turning of night into morning, of hesitation into decision — is where life actually happens. The dawn does not announce itself with trumpets. It arrives the way all important things arrive: gradually, then suddenly, then completely.

By the time the sun clears the horizon, the mystery has already ended. But for those few minutes, everything is still possible.
